sounds.intro: Akkadian has been dead for two thousand years, so every sound here is a reconstruction. Scholars work it out from how scribes used the cuneiform signs, from related Semitic languages such as Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic, from Akkadian words borrowed into other languages, and from a few late tablets that spell Akkadian in Greek letters. The consonants and vowel lengths are fairly secure; the emphatic sounds, the exact value of š and the stress are not.

rows.like: short and pure, as in Spanish or Italian

a trilled r, or perhaps one made at the back of the mouth

rows.note: Doubling matters: iparras 'he decides' doubles the r, iprus 'he decided' does not.

tips.p: ṣ, ṭ and q are the 'emphatic' consonants, a feature of all Semitic languages. Arabic says its emphatics with the throat tightened; Ethiopian languages say them as ejectives, with a sharp pop of air. Which way Akkadian went is unknown. Most teachers simply say them as s, t and k.

Long and short vowels are different sounds, and a word is only right with the right length: awīlum, not awilum. A macron (ā) marks a long vowel. Length often carries grammar: išpurū 'they sent' differs from išpur 'he sent' only by its long -ū.

When two vowels met, they merged into one long vowel, marked with a circumflex: rabium became rabûm 'great', and the vowel of iddâk 'he shall be killed' is two vowels run together. In transliteration the circumflex tells you two vowels once stood there.

Old Babylonian nouns and adjectives end in -m: šarrum, šarram, šarrim. After about 1500 BC the -m fell away (šarru), so mimation is one way to tell an Old Babylonian text from a later one like the Standard Babylonian Gilgameš.

Cuneiform writes syllables, and scribes often skipped doubled consonants and long vowels: i-la-ku for illaku 'he goes', a-wi-lum for awīlum, iš-pu-ru for išpurū. Sometimes they spelled them out, with an extra vowel (ma-a-ad for mād 'much') or a doubled consonant (id-di-in for iddin). The forms in this course come from comparing many spellings with the grammar.

Old Babylonian signs did not separate related sounds well: one sign writes ga and qá, another da and ṭa, another ki and qí, and ZA writes both za and ṣa. The reader chose the right value from the word.

No ancient source says where the stress fell. A common modern convention stresses the last long syllable before the end, one with a long vowel or ending in a consonant: a-WĪ-lum, i-PAR-ras. With no such syllable, stress the first: A-bum. A contracted vowel at the end takes the stress: ra-BÛM.

All of it, to some degree. Fairly sure: the consonants, vowel length and the case endings. Less sure: how the emphatics sounded, whether š and s were 'sh' and 's' or 's' and 'ts', how r was made, and where the stress fell.

grammar.title: Adjective and stative
grammar.note: An adjective follows its noun and copies its ending. With no ending at all it becomes the stative, which says 'is'.

grammar.title: Signs that are whole words
grammar.note: Logograms are Sumerian words read in Akkadian. Determinatives are silent signs that say what kind of word follows or precedes.

grammar.title: Pronoun suffixes
grammar.note: Possessive endings attach to a noun's short form. A similar set marks the object of a verb, as in liballiṭka 'may he keep you well'.

grammar.title: Independent pronouns
grammar.note: The verb already shows who acts, so these are added only for emphasis or in verbless sentences.

grammar.note: The first vowel of the class goes in the present and the perfect, the second in the preterite. In iṣṣabat the -t- of the perfect has merged with ṣ.

grammar.title: Numbers
grammar.note: 1 and 2 agree with their noun (feminine ištiat, šitta). From 3 to 10 the forms below go with feminine nouns, and masculine nouns take a form with -t (šalāšat). Numbers were rarely spelled out, so some readings are uncertain.

grammar.title: Weights and grain measures
grammar.note: Silver was weighed and barley measured by volume. Modern values are approximate and varied over time.

grammar.title: Prepositions and conjunctions
grammar.note: Prepositions take the genitive. inūma, ištu, adi and aššum can also begin a clause, whose verb is then in the subjunctive.

grammar.title: The subjunctive
grammar.note: A verb in a subordinate clause adds -u unless it already ends in a vowel. The negative there is lā, not ul.

grammar.title: Commands and wishes: šapārum
grammar.note: The imperative is for 'you'; the precative (li-, lu-) for everyone else. A prohibition uses lā with the present.

grammar.title: The stative: šalāmum 'to be well'
grammar.note: The stative describes a state. With lū it makes a wish: lū šalmāta 'may you be well'.
